phonemes.desc: Voiceless alveolar sibilant [s], as in English 'sea'
Short close front [i]; the first syllable carries the stress
Medial voiced velar fricative [ɣ]; between vowels Old Norse g softened to a glide, closer to the Spanish g of 'lago' than a hard stop
Short [u], alveolar trill [r], the voiced dental fricative [ð] — the soft 'th' of 'father' — and the final nominative ending -r, syllabic after the eth

pronunciation.approximation: 'SIG-urthr' — stress the first syllable, soften the middle g almost to a glide, sound the ð as the soft 'th' of 'father', and let the final -r hang as a light voiced syllable; it is the Old Norse nominative ending, not a separate vowel.

pronunciation.note: Sigurðr is Tier 1: the eth ð is a distinctive letter the ASCII form loses, and the final -r preserves the Old Norse nominative ending that English drops entirely. Cleasby-Vigfusson (s.v. Sigurðr) and Zoëga (s.v. Sigurðr) record the form as the name of the Vǫlsung hero; the name compounds sigr, 'victory', with -vǫrðr, 'guardian', yielding 'victory-guardian', and answers to the continental German Siegfried.

domains.title: Victory, Dragon-Slaying, Heroism
domains.subtitle: The domain of Sigurðr
domains.lead:
In the norse tradition, Sigurðr governed victory, dragon-slaying, heroism. The name encodes a sphere of power that shaped ritual, narrative, and social order.

His is the northern form of the greatest heroic story the Germanic world ever told: the foster-son of a smith who reforged his father's shattered sword, the slayer of the dragon Fáfnir, the wooer of the valkyrie behind the flame, and the oath-brother destroyed by the very loyalty that made him great. What the Iliad is to Greece, the Vǫlsunga cycle is to the North.

cards.name: Gramr
cards.desc: The sword Óðinn thrust into the tree Barnstokkr and only Sigmundr could draw; shattered in his last battle, reforged by Reginn for the son who would avenge him.

cards.name: Fáfnir at Gnitaheiðr
cards.desc: The brother turned dragon by greed, slain by a hero lying in a trench; from his heart-blood Sigurðr learned the speech of birds.

cards.name: The Flame-Wall
cards.desc: Through the vafrlogi on Hindarfjall rode Grani's rider to wake Brynhildr, the valkyrie Óðinn had sunk in sleep — the oath sworn there could not survive the world of men.

cards.name: The Cursed Hoard
cards.desc: Andvari's gold, paid as weregild for Ótr and cursed at its surrender; every hand it passed through — Hreiðmarr, Fáfnir, Sigurðr, the Gjúkings — it brought to ruin.

symbols.name: Gramr
symbols.meaning: The reforged sword of Sigmundr, drawn from Barnstokkr and mended by Reginn; with it Sigurðr slew Fáfnir

symbols.name: Grani
symbols.meaning: The grey horse of Sleipnir's line who bore Sigurðr through the flame-wall and carried the dragon's gold from Gnitaheiðr

symbols.name: Andvaranautr and the hoard
symbols.meaning: The dwarf Andvari's ring and gold, taken as ransom and cursed at the taking — the engine of every death in the cycle

symbols.name: The dragon's heart-blood
symbols.meaning: Roasting Fáfnir's heart, Sigurðr tasted the blood and understood the birds — knowledge bought from the monster he killed

symbols.name: The vafrlogi flame-wall
symbols.meaning: The ring of fire around the sleeping Brynhildr, crossable only by the destined rider; crossed twice, once for love and once in betrayal

mythology.lead: Sigurðr is the dragonslayer of the Vǫlsunga cycle, the Norse original of the German Siegfried and the last great hero of the legendary North. Son of Sigmundr and Hjǫrdís, fostered by the smith Reginn, he reforged his father's sword, killed the dragon Fáfnir, and woke the valkyrie Brynhildr from her enchanted sleep — then lost her, and his life, to a draught of forgetfulness and the plotting of his sworn brothers. His story survives in the Poetic Edda, the Prose Edda, and Vǫlsunga saga, and through the Middle High German Nibelungenlied it became the backbone of Wagner's Ring. Where the gods of the Edda face a doom they know is coming, Sigurðr faces one he has forgotten — and that is the more human tragedy.

myths.title: The Reforging of Gramr
myths.text:
At the wedding feast of his sister Signý, a one-eyed stranger — Óðinn himself — thrust a sword to the hilt into the tree Barnstokkr that grew through the hall of Vǫlsungr, and only Sigmundr of all the company could draw it. Years later Sigmundr fell in battle, the sword shattering beneath him against the same god's spear, and his widow Hjǫrdís carried the shards away for her unborn son. That son, Sigurðr, was fostered by Reginn, a smith of the dwarf-kin, who urged him against the dragon Fáfnir and forged blade after blade that broke under the boy's testing.

Only the shards of his father's sword held. Reginn reforged them into Gramr, and Sigurðr clove the smith's anvil to the stock and sheared a tuft of wool drifting downstream as though it were stone. The episode binds the hero to Óðinn from birth: the god who gave the sword also broke it, and the blade that passes from father to son is the visible thread of a destiny the boy never chose.

myths.title: The Slaying of Fáfnir
myths.text:
Fáfnir was Reginn's brother, who killed their father Hreiðmarr for the hoard paid as weregild for the slain Ótr and crawled away to Gnitaheiðr, where greed long brooding over gold twisted him into a dragon. Guided by a one-eyed old man, Sigurðr dug a trench across the dragon's path to the water and lay in it; when Fáfnir crawled overhead, he thrust Gramr upward into the heart. The dying dragon questioned his slayer and warned him that the gold would be his death — a warning Sigurðr answered with the hero's creed that every man must die, and wealth must serve until that day.

Roasting the dragon's heart for Reginn, Sigurðr burned his finger and set it in his mouth, and the heart-blood opened the speech of birds to him: the nuthatches in the branches warned that Reginn meant to kill him. He cut off the smith's head, loaded the cursed hoard onto Grani, and rode away the richest and most doomed man in the North. The birds that save him here will not be there at the end.

myths.title: The Ale of Forgetfulness
myths.text:
Sigurðr rode through the vafrlogi, the flame-wall on Hindarfjall, and woke Brynhildr, the valkyrie Óðinn had pricked with the sleep-thorn; they plighted their troth and parted. At the court of Gjúki's sons, the queen Grímhildr brewed him the ale of forgetfulness, and Brynhildr passed from his mind as if she had never been. He married Guðrún, swore oaths with her brothers Gunnarr and Hǫgni, and when Gunnarr sought Brynhildr's hand and could not cross the flames, Sigurðr exchanged shapes with him and rode the fire in his likeness — wooing his own forgotten beloved for another man, with a drawn sword laid between them in the bed.

The deception could not hold. Brynhildr learned from a ring and a quarrel at the river what had been done, and wounded in her pride she demanded Sigurðr's death. The brothers, bound to him by oath, incited the unsworn Guthormr, who stabbed Sigurðr as he slept; some lays — Sigurðarkviða en skamma and Guðrún's own laments — have him slain instead out of doors, in the forest. The texts disagree on the place but not on the meaning: the hoard's curse had reached the man who thought himself above it, through the only weapon that could touch him, the trust of those he called his own.

syncretism: Sigurðr is the northern twin of a pan-Germanic hero. The continental tradition — preserved in the Middle High German Nibelungenlied (c. 1200), the Lied vom Hürnen Seyfrid, and the Old Norse Þiðreks saga, which repatriates German material — tells of the same dragon-fight, hoard, and betrayal under the name Siegfried, with the details reworked: the valkyrie becomes a Burgundian queen, the flame-wall drops away, and the murder moves to a forest spring. Scholars have long read the cycle's skeleton against history, seeing in Gunnarr and the fall of the Gjúkings the shadow of the Burgundian kingdom destroyed by the Huns in 437 — legend crystallized around remembered catastrophe. The dragon-slaying itself belongs to a still older inheritance: the Indo-European formula of the hero who kills the serpent, traced by Calvert Watkins through Indra and Vṛtra, Herakles and the Lernaean hydra, and Beowulf's fatal last fight. In later folklore the story lived on in the Faroese Sjúrðar kvæði ballads, still sung and danced in the islands centuries after the saga manuscripts were copied.
culturalLegacy: No Norse figure has had a longer second life. William Morris retold the cycle in his epic The Story of Sigurd the Volsung and the Fall of the Niblungs (1876), which he called the great story of the North that should be to all his race what the tale of Troy was to the Greeks. Richard Wagner made it the armature of Der Ring des Nibelungen — Siegfried and Götterdämmerung follow the Norse sources where the Nibelungenlied had softened them, restoring the valkyrie Brünnhilde to the centre. Arthur Rackham's illustrations fixed the cycle's visual grammar for a century, and J. R. R. Tolkien, who read the Eddas closely, composed his own The Legend of Sigurd and Gudrún in Eddic metre. The dragonslayer persists in opera houses, novels, games, and film wherever a hero wins gold and is destroyed by it. In modern heathenry Sigurðr is honoured less as an object of cult than as the model of the heroic ethic — courage held fast inside a fate already written — and the runestones that depict him are among the tradition's most cited monuments. Restoring Sigurðr in Unicode keeps the eth and the nominative -r that the German Siegfried and the anglicized Sigurd alike have lost.
extendedMeditation: Names are not merely labels; they are compressed worlds. Sigurðr carries within it a norse understanding of victory under guard: sigr, the thing won, held by a vǫrðr, a watcher — as if the North already knew that every victory needs defending, and that the guard can fail. The hero who bore the name guarded the hoard, the oath, and the bride, and lost all three to a single draught of ale; the name outlived the man by eight centuries and counting. Unicode restoration returns that world to readable form: the eth that softens the ending, the final -r that marks him as the subject of his own sentence.

archaeology: The Sigurðr cycle is the most widely depicted heroic legend of the Viking Age. The Ramsund carving (Sö 101) in Södermanland, Sweden, shows the whole Gnitaheiðr episode in one frame — Sigurðr piercing the serpent from below, the heart roasting over the fire, the thumb in his mouth, the listening birds, the headless Reginn, and Grani laden with the gold — and the nearby Gök stone (Sö 327) quotes the same scene within a runic serpent band. The Drävle runestone (U 1163) in Uppland adds a further Swedish depiction, while across the North Sea the Manx cross-slabs, above all the Kirk Andreas cross, show Sigurðr roasting Fáfnir's heart, proof the legend travelled with Norse settlers. In Norway the carved portal of Hylestad stave church (c. 1200) narrates the cycle panel by panel, from the forging of Gramr to Reginn's death. The textual tradition is Icelandic and later: the heroic lays of the Poetic Edda survive chiefly in the Codex Regius (GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270), whose famous eight-leaf lacuna has cost us the fullest form of the Sigurðr lays — Brot af Sigurðarkviðu preserves only a fragment — while Vǫlsunga saga itself (c. 1270) survives in paper copies of the lost vellum NKS 1824 b 4to.
originalScriptNote: The medieval Norse wrote Sigurðr in the Latin alphabet the Icelanders adapted for their vernacular, and it is in that script — Codex Regius, the Vǫlsunga saga manuscripts — that the name is preserved. The hero's own age wrote in the Younger Futhark, the sixteen-rune alphabet carved on the memorial stones that depict his deeds; reduced to sixteen signs, it did not even distinguish ð from þ or d from t, so the full sound of the name was never recoverable from runes alone. The restored form Sigurðr keeps both features the Latin-script manuscripts attest: the eth ð, the voiced dental fricative, and the nominative ending -r. As a registrable domain the Unicode form carries the eth that the ASCII sigurd flattens to d — the punycode encodes exactly what the saga scribes wrote.
